Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Opinion Twice billed for dirty state databases Source : Sitsofe Mensah, Solutionist and Technology Associate with IMANIAfrica 26 November 2026 10:28am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
At 2:26 pm on 24 November 2026, a speed camera flashed along a northern highway. A commercial minivan wearing a 2026 Greater Accra plate, GT [REDACTED]-26, clocked 85 km/h in a 50 km/h zone. Hours later, Police MTTD dispatched a GH¢240.00 speeding ticket through TraffiTech-GH.
The SMS landed on an innocent citizen’s personal phone. He had never owned that commercial minivan, was not driving, and stood miles from that highway.
Puzzled, he tapped the link inside the GPS-MTTD text message. Without asking for a PIN or plate check, the portal opened a stranger’s traffic record on his screen.
There sat another man’s full name, commercial plate, ten-digit mobile number, and five-decimal highway coordinates. All four identifiers are masked in this essay. State platforms have broadcast enough private data for one week.
Whenever public databases misfire, defenders of state IT projects usually blame dusty legacy folders. That alibi dies on the rear bumper of this minivan.
The yellow commercial plate ends in -26. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA) issued it this year, deep inside Ghana’s mandatory Ghana Card era.
Parliament mandates DVLA under Section 3(1)(k) of Act 569 to keep accurate vehicle registers. The Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519) reinforce that duty with paid physical inspections. Private motorists renew road use certificates annually, while commercial vans return every six months
At every renewal, vehicle owners queue at testing bays, pay statutory fees, and present Ghana Cards under L.I. 2111. Since 2 November 2026, L.I. 2523 has tightened that rule with live biometric matching. Still, DVLA accepted an unverified ten-digit phone number on a 2026 commercial registration.
Meanwhile, pre-2023 vehicle owners face an extra GH¢25 fee to digitally onboard existing records ahead of 2027 plate changes. Motorists must make separate trips carrying registration certificates that DVLA itself printed and holds by law, and vehicle import documents. Drivers pay once to register a car, then pay again to digitise DVLA’s own paperwork.
Charging fresh fees to clean older archives rings hollow while the 2026 intake pours unverified numbers into the same register. A five-pesewa One-Time Password (OTP) at the registration desk would have stopped that wrong number cold.
Police guidelines note that back-office officers review camera photographs before issuing tickets under Act 1153. Staring harder at a bumper photo cannot rescue a corrupted DVLA phone field.
Trace the fallout for both men tied to that single database entry.
DVLA captured the subscriber’s mobile number indirectly from a third party without his knowledge. That breaches direct-collection limits in Section 21 and accuracy duties in Section 26 of the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843). Serving a statutory penalty on an uninvolved citizen’s line also violated Sections 18 and 20.
Across town, the actual van keeper had his identity, route, and alleged offence exposed to a stranger. Official Police advisories warn citizens never to tap links inside SMS messages. Yet the GPS-MTTD message opened his dossier unchallenged, leaking special personal data protected under Sections 28, 30, 37, and 96.
Crime-prevention exemptions in Sections 60 and 61 of Act 843 never pardon weak security controls or third-party leaks. Under Section 31, both DVLA and GPS-MTTD owe formal breach notices to the Data Protection Commission and that vehicle keeper.
At the foot of the TraffiTech-GH citation sits a small yellow box. If the matched register details are not yours, it shrugs, “contest the fine and say so”.
Article 23 of the 1992 Constitution binds administrative bodies to act fairly and reasonably. The ticket gives 14 days to pay GH¢240.00, after which Regulation 242 of L.I. 2519 adds a 1 per cent daily surcharge. Disputing it requires an online filing, a regional MTTD station appointment, and a court date.
How did DVLA’s skipped five-second check become an innocent citizen’s multi-day errand? Meanwhile, the real commercial keeper remains legally unserved, walking blind towards DVLA service blocks after 9 December.
Even a verified phone number at first registration decays over time. Mobile networks routinely deactivate dormant SIM cards after six months of inactivity and resell those numbers to new Ghana Card holders. When SIM owners switch lines or let secondary phones numbers lapse, strangers legally inherit their old digits.
Section 26 of Data Protection Act 843 requires state controllers to keep personal data up to date, not merely accurate on day one. Commercial vans already visit the DVLA every six months for paid inspections, matching the telecom industry’s six-month churn cycle.
Failing to re-check SIM ownership against the keeper’s Ghana Card turns every recycled number into a waiting data breach. Live matching between the NCA Central SIM Register and NIA records must therefore run before any ticket leaves TraffiTech-GH.
Public confidence erodes fastest when state referees ignore the rules they enforce on private businesses. Last month, the Data Protection Commission flagged six firms in Kaneshie and Tudu and summoned them before CID. When state registries leak offence records or fire blind citations, that regulatory voice drops to a murmur.
Basic engineering hygiene must precede any expansion of TraffiTech-GH into automated insurance and roadworthiness fines. DVLA should block any phone number from entering the vehicle register without live SMS OTP confirmation and NIA-linked SIM verification.
On the policing side, GPS-MTTD and its NIB payment portal must gate every citation behind a plate or Ghana Card challenge. The Data Protection Commission should simultaneously audit both controllers under Section 31 and publish its remediation timeline.
Sharp highway cameras cannot rescue a careless licensing counter. When the logbook inside the registration hall is crooked, faster software simply delivers state errors to innocent phones on time.
